core.q: Section 608 of which federal law governs refrigerant handling in the United States?
core.explain: Section 608 belongs to the Clean Air Act. It requires anyone who maintains, services, repairs, or disposes of equipment with regulated refrigerant to be certified.

core.q: What atmospheric layer is damaged by chlorine released from CFC and HCFC refrigerants?
core.explain: Chlorine atoms released from CFCs and HCFCs break down stratospheric ozone. A single chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules before it becomes inactive.

core.q: The international agreement that first set a timetable for phasing out ozone-depleting substances is the:
core.explain: The Montreal Protocol (1987) established the global phase-out schedule for CFCs and HCFCs that U.S. law implements domestically through the Clean Air Act.

core.q: A refrigerant release of what quantity or less is exempt from mandatory recovery before opening the system?
core.explain: De minimis releases of 0.1 ounce or less — such as the small amount lost when connecting or disconnecting gauge hoses — do not trigger the recovery requirement.

core.q: Which term describes cleaning refrigerant on-site for reuse in the same system or another appliance owned by the same person, without reaching the purity of new product?
core.explain: Recycling reduces moisture, acidity, and particulates but does not test to the ARI 700 purity standard used for reclaimed refrigerant.

core.q: Reclaimed refrigerant must be processed and chemically tested to meet which purity standard before it can be sold as new product?
core.explain: Reclamation restores refrigerant to the AHRI (formerly ARI) 700 purity specification, verified by chemical analysis, typically at an off-site facility.

core.q: If a technician finds a leak that requires repair, how many days do they generally have to complete the repair?
core.explain: Leaks generally must be repaired within 30 days of discovery, unless the owner files a retrofit or retire plan, which extends the deadline to one year.

core.q: If an owner instead chooses to retrofit or retire a leaking appliance rather than repair it, the work must be completed within:
core.explain: A documented retrofit or retire plan must be kept on site, and the retrofit or retirement must be completed within one year of the leak being discovered.

core.q: Which class of substances did the 1992 production and import prohibition first cover?
core.explain: The July 1, 1992 prohibition targeted CFCs and HCFCs. HFCs were added to venting-prohibition coverage later, on November 15, 1995.

core.q: Under Section 608, it is illegal to knowingly vent which category of refrigerants to the atmosphere during service, maintenance, repair, or disposal?
options: Any substitute or regulated refrigerant, including HFCs and HFOs
core.explain: The venting prohibition applies broadly to ozone-depleting refrigerants and their substitutes, including HFCs and HFO blends — not just the original CFC/HCFC classes.

type1.q: Type I certification covers small appliances that are hermetically sealed, factory-charged, and contain how much refrigerant?
type1.explain: Type I applies to small appliances such as refrigerators, freezers, window air conditioners, dehumidifiers, and vending machines with a factory charge of 5 lbs or less.

type1.q: Which of these is NOT typically classified as a Type I small appliance?
type1.explain: Rooftop units are high-pressure commercial equipment, covered under Type II — not the small, hermetically sealed appliances covered by Type I.

type1.q: For small appliances manufactured AFTER November 15, 1993, what is the minimum recovery efficiency required when the compressor is operating?
type1.explain: Post-1993 equipment requires recovering 90% of the refrigerant charge when the compressor is functional, or 80% if it is not, or evacuating the system to 4 inches of Hg vacuum.

type1.q: For small appliances manufactured BEFORE November 15, 1993, what recovery percentage is required regardless of whether the compressor works?
type1.explain: Older equipment (pre-1993) only requires 80% recovery whether or not the compressor is operational, or evacuation to 4 inches Hg vacuum.

type1.q: Passive recovery is best described as:
options: Recovery using the appliance's own working compressor to push refrigerant into a recovery container
Recovery using a separate, self-contained recovery machine with its own compressor
Recovery performed only by reclaiming facilities
type1.explain: Passive (system-dependent) recovery relies on the appliance's own compressor. If that compressor doesn't work, active recovery equipment with an independent compressor must be used instead.

type1.q: Active recovery equipment is defined by having:
options: Its own self-contained compressor, separate from the appliance being serviced
A requirement to be manufactured before 1993
type1.explain: Active recovery machines carry their own compressor, allowing recovery even when the appliance's built-in compressor has failed.

type1.q: Which EPA 608 exam section is the only one that a certifying organization may administer as an open-book test?
type1.explain: Type I is unique in that it may be offered open-book, including online proctored formats, making it the most accessible entry point for new technicians.

type1.q: Is leak repair legally mandatory for small (Type I) appliances?
options: No, but repair is recommended whenever practical
type1.explain: Unlike larger equipment, small appliances are not subject to a mandatory leak-repair deadline, though repairing leaks whenever possible is still good practice.

type1.q: A technician recovering refrigerant from a small appliance with a non-functional compressor, manufactured in 2005, must recover at least:
type1.explain: With the compressor inoperative on post-1993 equipment, the requirement drops to 80% recovery, or the technician may instead pull a 4 inch Hg vacuum.

type1.q: Which of the following requires certification to purchase regulated refrigerant for small appliance service?
options: Any of Type I, Type II, Type III, or Universal, matching the equipment worked on
No certification is required for small appliances
type1.explain: A technician needs the certification matching the equipment category — Type I for small appliances — before purchasing regulated refrigerant for that work.

type2.q: Type II covers high-pressure appliances using refrigerants with a boiling point in what range at atmospheric pressure?
type2.explain: High-pressure refrigerants such as R-22, R-410A, R-404A, and R-407C have boiling points between -50°C and 10°C at atmospheric pressure, distinguishing them from Type III's low-pressure refrigerants.

type2.q: Which of these systems would typically require Type II (or Universal) certification to service?
type2.explain: Residential split systems, heat pumps, and rooftop commercial units run on high-pressure refrigerants and fall under Type II.

type2.q: On recovery equipment manufactured after November 15, 1993, a Type II system holding LESS than 200 lbs of refrigerant must generally be evacuated to what vacuum level?
type2.explain: Post-1993 recovery equipment must pull systems under 200 lbs down to roughly 4 inches Hg vacuum before the system may be opened.

type2.q: For very-high-pressure refrigerants like R-410A, R-404A, and R-507, why does EPA guidance set the target near 0 psig rather than a deep vacuum?
options: These refrigerants are non-regulated so no target applies
Pulling a deep vacuum on these blends risks freezing residual moisture and damaging system components
It is faster to reach 0 psig
These refrigerants cannot be recovered at all
type2.explain: Very-high-pressure blends are prone to moisture freeze-out under deep vacuum, so recovery targets for these are set closer to atmospheric (0 psig) rather than a deep inches-Hg vacuum.

type2.q: What must a technician hold before purchasing Type II refrigerant to recover it from a rooftop commercial unit?
options: A Type II or Universal certification
A state HVAC contractor license only
type2.explain: Federal law requires Type II or Universal EPA 608 certification specifically to purchase and handle high-pressure refrigerants — a state contractor license does not substitute for it.

type2.q: Which of these is a common Type II refrigerant used in residential split systems and heat pumps?
type2.explain: R-410A is a common high-pressure refrigerant used across modern residential split systems and heat pumps, and falls under Type II.

type2.q: The distinction between Type II and Type III refrigerants is primarily based on:
type2.explain: Type classifications hinge on the refrigerant's boiling point at atmospheric pressure, which determines whether the system runs at high pressure (Type II) or below atmospheric pressure (Type III).

type2.q: General safety practice for Type II high-pressure work includes:
options: Working without eye protection since refrigerant is odorless
Using proper PPE, ensuring adequate ventilation, and respecting refrigerant safety group ratings
Venting excess refrigerant to speed up the job
type2.explain: High-pressure refrigerant work carries burn, frostbite, and asphyxiation risk, so PPE, ventilation, and awareness of refrigerant safety classifications are core exam topics.

type2.q: A technician measures the vacuum on a Type II system after recovery and reads it in inches of Hg. What does this unit tell you about the section being tested?
options: It signals Type II content, since Type III uses mm Hg absolute instead
It is irrelevant to certification type
It only applies to Core questions
type2.explain: Inches of Hg vacuum is the unit used for high-pressure (Type II) evacuation levels, while Type III low-pressure systems are measured in mm Hg absolute — a common exam unit trap.

type2.q: Leak rate thresholds that can trigger mandatory repair obligations apply to appliances holding at least how much refrigerant?
options: There is no minimum charge size
type2.explain: Mandatory annual leak-rate repair triggers generally apply to appliances with a full charge of 50 lbs or more of refrigerant.

type3.q: Type III covers low-pressure appliances using refrigerants with a boiling point at atmospheric pressure that is:
type3.explain: Low-pressure refrigerants such as R-11 and R-123, common in large chillers, boil above 10°C at atmospheric pressure — the opposite end of the spectrum from Type II.

type3.q: Type III equipment most commonly refers to which kind of system?
type3.explain: Type III certification centers on low-pressure chillers, typically found in large commercial and industrial cooling plants.

type3.q: Because low-pressure chillers operate below atmospheric pressure, the main contamination risk during normal operation is:
options: Refrigerant venting to atmosphere under pressure
Air and moisture infiltrating into the system
type3.explain: Since the system runs below atmospheric pressure, any leak tends to pull air and moisture IN rather than push refrigerant out — a key conceptual difference from high-pressure systems.

type3.q: Required evacuation for Type III low-pressure appliances is expressed in which unit?
type3.explain: Type III evacuation levels are given in millimeters of mercury, absolute — a distinct unit from the inches-of-Hg-vacuum figures used for Type II, and a frequent point of confusion on the exam.

type3.q: The standard evacuation target commonly cited for Type III low-pressure systems is approximately:
type3.explain: 25 mm Hg absolute is the commonly referenced Type III evacuation target — always confirm the exact figure against your certifying organization's current chart before the exam.

type3.q: Which of these refrigerants is associated with low-pressure (Type III) chiller applications?
type3.explain: R-123 is a low-pressure HCFC refrigerant historically used in centrifugal chillers, placing it under Type III rather than Type II.

type3.q: Reading '25 mm Hg' on a Type III exam question versus '25 inches Hg' on a Type II question illustrates why technicians should:
options: Ignore units since the numbers are similar
Always double-check the unit of measure before selecting an answer
Assume mm Hg and inches Hg are interchangeable
type3.explain: Mixing up mm Hg absolute and inches Hg vacuum is one of the most common exam traps between Type II and Type III questions — units carry real meaning, not just decoration.

type3.q: Which general safety concern is heightened on low-pressure chiller work compared to sealed high-pressure systems?
options: Risk of the system exploding under pressure
Increased chance of air and moisture contamination requiring careful evacuation before recharge
No safety concerns apply to low-pressure systems
type3.explain: Because these systems operate under vacuum, thorough evacuation and moisture control before recharging are critical safety and performance concerns unique to Type III work.

type3.q: To earn Universal certification, a technician must pass:
options: Core, Type I, Type II, and Type III
Any two of the four sections
type3.explain: Universal certification requires passing all four sections — Core, Type I, Type II, and Type III — each with its own passing score.

type3.q: If a technician has already passed Core and Type II, and later passes Type I and Type III, what happens to their certification?
options: Nothing, they must retake all four together
It automatically upgrades to Universal once all four sections are passed
They must apply for a completely new certificate number
Universal is not available this way
type3.explain: Section 608 certification can be built up over time — once Core plus all three Type sections are passed, credentials upgrade to Universal automatically.
